claim: The pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by SARS-CoV-2 has affected more than 10 million people, including pregnant women.
source: The pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) has affected more than 10 million people, including pregnant women.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scale of the pandemic at the time of writing, representing established knowledge about COVID-19 case numbers.

claim: No consistent evidence for vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 exists.
source: To date, no consistent evidence for the vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 exists.
evidence: This statement summarizes the state of scientific knowledge at the time of publication regarding vertical transmission.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 canonically utilizes the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor and the serine protease TMPRSS2 for cell entry.
source: The novel coronavirus canonically utilizes the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor and the serine protease TMPRSS2 for cell entry.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 cell entry mechanisms, widely accepted in the field.

claim: Co-transcription of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is negligible in the placenta.
source: We report that co-transcription of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is negligible in the placenta, thus not a likely path of vertical transmission for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on single-cell/nuclei RNA-sequencing data analysis.

claim: Receptors for Zika virus and cytomegalovirus are highly expressed by placental cell types.
source: By contrast, receptors for Zika virus and cytomegalovirus, which cause congenital infections, are highly expressed by placental cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis comparing expression of different viral receptors.

claim: The placenta minimally expresses the canonical cell-entry mediators for SARS-CoV-2.
source: These data show that the placenta minimally expresses the canonical cell-entry mediators for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the RNA-sequencing data presented.

claim: The placenta serves as the lungs, gut, kidneys, and liver of the fetus.
source: The placenta serves as the lungs, gut, kidneys, and liver of the fetus (Burton and Jauniaux, 2015; Maltepe and Fisher, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The placenta has major biological actions that modulate maternal physiology.
source: This fetal organ also has major biological actions that modulate maternal physiology (Burton and Jauniaux, 2015; Sasaki and Norwitz, 2011; Taglauer et al., 2014; Fitzgerald et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The placenta and chorioamniotic membranes shield the fetus against microbes from hematogenous dissemination and from invading the amniotic cavity.
source: and, importantly, together with the extraplacental chorioamniotic membranes, shield the fetus against microbes from hematogenous dissemination and from invading the amniotic cavity (Ander et al., 2019; Kwon et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most pathogens that cause hematogenous infections in the mother cannot reach the fetus due to protective mechanisms provided by placental trophoblast cells.
source: Indeed, most pathogens that cause hematogenous infections in the mother cannot reach the fetus, which is largely due to the potent protective mechanisms provided by placental cells (i.e. trophoblast cells: syncytiotrophoblasts and cytotrophoblasts) (Parry et al., 1997; Koi et al., 2002; Arora et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Toxoplasma gondii, Rubella virus, herpesvirus (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Zika virus are capable of crossing the placenta and infecting the fetus, causing congenital disease.
source: Yet, some of these pathogens such as Toxoplasma gondii, Rubella virus, herpesvirus (HSV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Zika virus (ZIKV), among others, are capable of crossing the placenta and infecting the fetus, thus causing congenital disease (Stegmann and Carey, 2002; Coyne and Lazear, 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A local outbreak of pneumonia caused by SARS-CoV-2 was reported in Wuhan, China in December 2019.
source: In December 2019, a local outbreak of pneumonia caused by a novel coronavirus—severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)—was reported in Wuhan (Hubei, China) (Dong et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature documenting the outbreak.

claim: After exposure to SARS-CoV-2, susceptible individuals can develop COVID-19 with symptoms ranging from fever and cough to severe respiratory illness, and in some cases it is life-threatening.
source: After exposure to SARS-COV-2, susceptible individuals can develop coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) consisting of symptoms that may range from fever and cough to severe respiratory illness; in some cases, COVID-19 is life-threatening (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020a; Wadman, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to CDC and other sources.

claim: More than 10 million COVID-19 cases have been confirmed, accounting for more than 500,000 deaths.
source: Since the onset of the outbreak, more than 10 million COVID-19 cases have been confirmed, accounting for more than 500,000 deaths (COVID-19, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to COVID-19 data sources.

claim: By April 2019, New York and Michigan were the most severely affected states in the United States.
source: By April 2019, the states of New York and Michigan were the most severely affected (COVID-19, 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to COVID-19 data sources.

claim: The metropolitan areas of New York City and Detroit possess large populations subject to health disparities including limited access to health care, chronic exposure to pollution, and pre-existing cardiovascular conditions.
source: given that the metropolitan areas of New York City and Detroit possess large populations subject to health disparities that include limited access to health care, chronic exposure to pollution, and pre-existing cardiovascular conditions (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to CDC sources.

claim: Pregnant women and their fetuses represent a potential high-risk population in light of the COVID-19 outbreak.
source: Pregnant women and their fetuses represent a potential high-risk population in light of the COVID-19 outbreak (Dashraath et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Rasmussen et al., 2020; Ashokka et al., 2020; Della Gatta et al., 2020; Weber LeBrun et al., 2020; Tekbali, 2020; Vintzileos, 2020; Lokken, 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Viral infections such as influenza show increased severity in pregnant women.
source: given that viral infections such as influenza (Neuzil et al., 1998; Lindsay et al., 2006; Jamieson et al., 2006; Cervantes-Gonzalez and Launay, 2010; Pandemic H1N1 Influenza in Pregnancy Working Group et al., 2010; Mosby et al., 2011; Pazos et al., 2012; Raj et al., 2014), varicella (Triebwasser et al., 1967; Paryani and Arvin, 1986; Esmonde et al., 1989; Haake et al., 1990; Swamy and Dotters-Katz, 2019), Ebola (Olgun, 2018; Muehlenbachs et al., 2017), and measles (Christensen et al., 1954; Atmar et al., 1992) show increased severity in this physiological state.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV have severe effects in both the mother and the fetus, but vertical transmission has not been proven.
source: Other coronaviruses, such as SARS-CoV-1 and MERS-CoV, have severe effects in both the mother and the fetus, but vertical transmission has not been proven (Wong et al., 2004; Ng et al., 2006; Alserehi et al., 2016; Jeong et al., 2017)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Only ~15% of pregnant women test positive for SARS-CoV-2 and a small fraction of them are symptomatic.
source: By contrast with the above-mentioned viral infections, only ~15% of pregnant women test positive for SARS-CoV-2 and a small fraction of them are symptomatic (Sutton et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Most pregnant women with SARS-CoV-2 experience only a mild illness.
source: most of whom experience only a mild illness (Chen et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The clinical characteristics of pregnant women with COVID-19 appear similar to those of non-pregnant adults.
source: Consequently, the clinical characteristics of pregnant women with COVID-19 appear similar to those of non-pregnant adults (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Severe COVID-19 can lead to maternal death.
source: Yet, recent reports have shown that severe COVID-19 can lead to maternal death (Hantoushzadeh et al., 2020; Blitz, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No conclusive evidence of vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 has been generated.
source: However, thus far, no conclusive evidence of vertical transmission has been generated (Weber LeBrun et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b; Stower, 2020; Lamouroux et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2020; Siberry et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Infants born to mothers with COVID-19 test negative for SARS-CoV-2 and do not develop serious clinical symptoms.
source: Consistently, infants born to mothers with COVID-19 test negative for SARS-CoV-2, do not develop serious clinical symptoms (e.g., fever, cough, diarrhea, or abnormal radiologic or hematologic evidence), and are promptly discharged from the hospital (Chen et al., 2020c).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A small fraction of neonates born to women with COVID-19 tested positive for the virus at 1-4 days of life.
source: Case reports have shown that a small fraction of neonates born to women with COVID-19 tested positive for the virus at 1–4 days of life (Zeng et al., 2020a; Alzamora et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to case reports.

claim: Neonates who tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 at 1-4 days of life subsequently tested negative on day 6-7.
source: yet these neonates subsequently tested negative on day 6-7 (Zeng et al., 2020a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a case report.

claim: A few neonates born to mothers with COVID-19 had increased concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 IgM and IgG.
source: In addition, serological studies revealed that a few neonates born to mothers with COVID-19 had increased concentrations of SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin (Ig)M as well as IgG (Zeng et al., 2020b; Dong et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Elevated concentrations of IgG in neonates are likely due to passive transfer from the mother to the fetus across the placenta.
source: The elevated concentrations of IgG are likely due to the passive transfer of this immunoglobulin from the mother to the fetus across the placenta.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about IgG transfer across the placenta.

claim: Increased levels of IgM in neonates suggest that the fetus was infected with SARS-CoV-2 because IgM cannot cross the placenta due to its large molecular weight.
source: However, the increased levels of IgM suggest that the fetus was infected with SARS-CoV-2 given that this immunoglobulin cannot cross the placenta as a result of its large molecular weight.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about IgM properties and placental transfer.

claim: All neonates with elevated IgM tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 and did not present any symptoms.
source: Nonetheless, all neonates included in the above-mentioned studies tested negative for the virus and did not present any symptoms (Zeng et al., 2020b; Dong et al., 2020b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been detected in amniotic fluid from a woman who died of COVID-19.
source: In the first case report, the viral RNA was detected in amniotic fluid from a woman who was severely affected and died of COVID-19 (Zamaniyan, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a case report.

claim: A premature neonate from a woman who died of COVID-19 tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 after delivery but 24 hr later tested positive.
source: The premature neonate tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 after delivery but 24 hr later tested positive (Zamaniyan, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a case report.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in the placenta and umbilical cord from a woman with severe pre-eclampsia and placental abruption, yet none of the fetal tissues tested positive.
source: In the second case report, the viral RNA was detected in the placenta and umbilical cord from a woman with severe pre-eclampsia, placental abruption, and other complications, yet none of the fetal tissues tested positive (Hosier, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a case report.

claim: Cell entry and spread of SARS-CoV-2 are widely thought to depend on the ACE2 receptor.
source: Cell entry and the spread of SARS-CoV-2 are widely thought to depend on the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor (Shang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell entry and spread of SARS-CoV-2 are widely thought to depend on the serine protease TMPRSS2.
source: Cell entry and the spread of SARS-CoV-2 are widely thought to depend on the angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor (Shang et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020a) and the serine protease TMPRSS2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Very few cells co-express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in the human placenta throughout the three trimesters of pregnancy.
source: Strikingly, we found that very few cells co-express ACE2 and TMPRSS2 (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on single-cell RNA-sequencing data analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Using a threshold of one transcript per cell, only four cells with co-expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 were detected in any of the three trimesters, resulting in an estimated <1/10,000 cells.
source: Using a very permissive threshold of expression of one transcript per cell, only four cells with co-expression were detected in any of the three trimesters, resulting in an estimated <1/10,000 cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The first-trimester data showing minimal expression of ACE2 at the human maternal-fetal interface are in agreement with a prior report.
source: Our first-trimester data are in agreement with a prior report showing minimal expression of ACE2 at the human maternal-fetal interface (Zheng et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement compares the study's findings to prior literature.

claim: Co-expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 was minimally detected in the chorioamniotic membranes.
source: Again, co-expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 was minimally detected in the chorioamniotic membranes (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reported scRNA-seq studies of the human placenta contain a low fraction of syncytiotrophoblast cells due to dissociation bias.
source: This is likely the reason why the reported scRNA-seq studies of the human placenta contain a low fraction of syncytiotrophoblast cells [STB, multinucleated cells forming the outermost fetal component of the placenta in direct contact with the maternal circulation (i.e., intervillous space)] (Vento-Tormo et al., 2018; Pique-Regi et al., 2019; Tsang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on technical limitations of scRNA-seq and citations to prior studies.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA-seq reduces dissociation bias against large cells.
source: To address this possibility, we prepared single-nucleus suspensions of the placental tissues (including the decidua basalis) and performed single-nuclear RNAseq (snRNA-seq), which reduces the dissociation bias against large cells (Wu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature about snRNA-seq methodology.

claim: snRNA-seq is compatible with biobank-frozen samples.
source: An important advantage of snRNA-seq is its compatibility with biobank-frozen samples
evidence: This is established knowledge about snRNA-seq methodology.

claim: This study represents the first snRNA-seq study of the placental tissues.
source: This represents the first snRNA-seq study of the placental tissues.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's methodology.

claim: A larger fraction of syncytiotrophoblast cells/nuclei was observed using snRNA-seq compared to scRNA-seq.
source: As expected, a larger fraction of STB cells/nuclei was observed using snRNA-seq compared to scRNA-seq (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The snRNA-seq data demonstrated that co-expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is unlikely in the placental tissues.
source: Consistent with the scRNAseq analyses, the snRNAseq data demonstrated that co-expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is unlikely in the placental tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's snRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: snRNA-seq has a higher background compared to scRNA-seq.
source: A limitation of snRNA-seq is that it has a higher background compared to scRNAseq
evidence: This is established knowledge about the technical limitations of snRNA-seq.

claim: ACE2 was detected above background in most third-trimester placental tissue samples in microarray datasets.
source: These analyses of bulk gene expression data revealed that, while ACE2 was detected above background in most of the samples, TMPRSS2 was largely undetected (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of microarray data.

claim: TMPRSS2 was largely undetected in third-trimester placental tissues in microarray datasets.
source: These analyses of bulk gene expression data revealed that, while ACE2 was detected above background in most of the samples, TMPRSS2 was largely undetected (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis of microarray data.

claim: The human placental tissues negligibly co-express ACE2 and TMPRSS2.
source: Collectively, these results consistently indicate that the human placental tissues negligibly co-express ACE2 and TMPRSS2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of data from the study.

claim: The reduced expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in placenta contrasts with the high expression in nasal goblet and ciliated cells within the human airways, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract.
source: This reduced expression contrasts with the high expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 in nasal goblet and ciliated cells within the human airways, lungs, and gastrointestinal tract, which are targeted during COVID-19 (Muus, 2020; Wang, 2020b; HCA Lung Biological Network et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement compares the study's findings to prior literature about expression in other tissues.

claim: Vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is unlikely to occur unless facilitated by other concomitant pathological conditions resulting in a breach of the maternal-fetal crosstalk.
source: Therefore, our results suggest that vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2 is unlikely to occur unless facilitated by other concomitant pathological conditions resulting in a breach of the maternal-fetal crosstalk.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's data with speculation about possible exceptions.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 could potentially infect the human placenta by using alternate entry routes while interacting with other proteins.
source: There is a possibility, however, that SARS-CoV-2 could infect the human placenta by using alternate entry routes while interacting with other proteins (Gordon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative mechanisms, supported by a citation.

claim: In vitro studies suggest that BSG provides an alternate entry for SARS-CoV-2 when ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are not expressed.
source: For example, in vitro studies suggest that BSG (Basigin, also called CD147 or EMMPRIN, transmembrane glycoprotein belonging to the immunoglobulin superfamily) provides an alternate entry for SARS-CoV-2 when ACE2 and TMPRSS2 are not expressed (Blanco-Melo et al., 2020; Wang, 2020c; Ulrich and Pillat, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The placenta and chorioamniotic membranes expressed high levels of BSG throughout pregnancy.
source: We found that the placenta and chorioamniotic membranes expressed high levels of BSG throughout pregnancy (Figure 2, CoV-Alt)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: BSG is widely expressed in all human tissues and cell types.
source: yet this transcript is also widely expressed in all human tissues and cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: BSG alone is unlikely to be a sufficient requirement for SARS-CoV-2 viral entry.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that this protein alone is a sufficient requirement for SARS-CoV-2 viral entry, and other proteins may be required to explain the cell type primarily affected by COVID-19.
evidence: This is an inference based on the widespread expression of BSG and the specific cell tropism of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: Cathepsin L (CSTL) and FURIN may function as proteases priming the SARS-CoV-2 S protein.
source: Moreover, cathepsin L (CSTL) and FURIN may also function as proteases priming the SARS-CoV-2 S protein (Lukassen et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CSTL and FURIN are highly expressed by the placental tissues throughout gestation.
source: We found that these proteases are highly expressed by the placental tissues throughout gestation (Figure 2, CoV-Alt).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: CSTL and FURIN may not provide sufficient levels of priming by themselves when tested with SARS-CoV-1.
source: Nevertheless, these proteases may not provide sufficient levels of priming by themselves (Shirato et al., 2017; Shirato et al., 2018; Iwata-Yoshikawa et al., 2019) when tested with SARS-CoV-1
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature about SARS-CoV-1.

claim: The placental tissues are enriched in maternal and fetal macrophages.
source: Given that the placental tissues are enriched in maternal and fetal macrophages (Pique-Regi et al., 2019)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A subset of macrophages expressing sialoadhesin (SIGLEC1) can contribute to viral spread during SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: and that a subset of these immune cells expressing sialoadhesin (SIGLEC1, also known as CD169) can contribute to viral spread during SARS-CoV-2 infection (Chen, 2020; Park, 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SIGLEC1 was expressed by macrophages in the placenta and chorioamniotic membranes and, to a lesser extent, in T cells.
source: As expected, SIGLEC1 was expressed by macrophages in the placenta and chorioamniotic membranes and, to a lesser extent, in T cells (Figure 2, CoV-Alt).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Even if the virus could infect placental/decidual macrophages expressing SIGLEC1, this is not sufficient for viral spreading.
source: However, even if the virus could infect the placental/decidual macrophages expressing SIGLEC1, this is not sufficient for viral spreading.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements for viral spreading.

claim: ADAM17 is a metalloproteinase that competes with TMPRSS2 in ACE2 processing.
source: The expression of ADAM17 was also investigated in the placental tissues as this metalloproteinase competes with TMPRSS2 in ACE2 processing (Heurich et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The placenta and chorioamniotic membranes highly expressed ADAM17.
source: The placenta and chorioamniotic membranes highly expressed ADAM17 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only cleavage by TMPRSS2 results in augmented SARS-S-driven cell entry.
source: however, only cleavage by TMPRSS2 results in augmented SARS-S-driven cell entry (Heurich et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: CoV-Alt molecules are likely to be less efficient than ACE2 and TMPRSS2 for SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: While these CoV-Alt molecules may be used for SARS-CoV-2 infection, they are likely to be less efficient than ACE2 and TMPRSS2, which are already targeted for antiviral interventions (Hoffmann et al., 2020)
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Known receptors for CMV include NRP2, PDFGRA, and CD46.
source: Known receptors for CMV include NRP2 (Martinez-Martin et al., 2018), PDFGRA (Martinez-Martin et al., 2018), and CD46 (Stein et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: All CMV receptors (NRP2, PDFGRA, and CD46) were highly expressed in several placental cell types.
source: Notably, all of these receptors were highly expressed in several placental cell types (Figure 2, CMV and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: AXL is the preferred receptor for ZIKV.
source: Next, we investigated the expression of the AXL receptor for ZIKV (Richard et al., 2017; Persaud et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: AXL was highly expressed by the cells of the human placenta and chorioamniotic membranes throughout gestation.
source: Consistent with vertical transmission, AXL, the preferred receptor for ZIKV, was highly expressed by the cells of the human placenta and chorioamniotic membranes throughout gestation (Figure 2, ZIKV).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The expression of CD209 was mainly found in the maternal and fetal macrophage subsets.
source: The expression of CD209 was mainly found in the maternal and fetal macrophage subsets, as expected (Svensson et al., 2011; Swieboda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis, consistent with citations to prior literature.

claim: The expression of TYRO3 was low in placental tissues.
source: Yet, the expression of TYRO3 was low (Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TAM receptors are not essential for ZIKV infection.
source: consistent with the view that TAM receptors are not essential for ZIKV infection (Hastings et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is unlikely to infect the placenta and fetus since its canonical receptor and protease, ACE2 and TMPRSS2, are only minimally expressed by the human placenta throughout pregnancy.
source: In conclusion, the single-cell transcriptomic analysis presented herein provides evidence that SARS-CoV-2 is unlikely to infect the placenta and fetus since its canonical receptor and protease, ACE2 and TMPRSS2, are only minimally expressed by the human placenta throughout pregnancy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the data presented.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 receptors are not expressed by the chorioamniotic membranes in the third trimester.
source: In addition, we showed that the SARS-CoV-2 receptors are not expressed by the chorioamniotic membranes in the third trimester.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Viral receptors utilized by CMV, ZIKV, and others are highly expressed by the human placental tissues.
source: However, viral receptors utilized by CMV, ZIKV, and others are highly expressed by the human placental tissues.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's data analysis.

claim: The data indicate a low likelihood of placental infection and vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
source: While transcript levels do not always correlate with protein expression, our data indicate a low likelihood of placental infection and vertical transmission of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's data with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: It is possible that the expression of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 is much higher in individuals with pregnancy complications related to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which can alter the expression of ACE2.
source: However, it is still possible that the expression of these proteins is much higher in individuals with pregnancy complications related to the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), which can alter the expression of ACE2 (Herse et al., 2007; Alexandre et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible exceptions, supported by citations.

claim: The cellular receptors and mechanisms that could be exploited by SARS-CoV-2 are still under investigation.
source: The cellular receptors and mechanisms that could be exploited by SARS-CoV-2 are still under investigation (Gordon et al., 2020)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to ongoing research.

claim: Single-cell atlases can help to identify cell types with a similar transcriptional profile to those that are known to participate in COVID-19.
source: yet single-cell atlases can help to identify cell types with a similar transcriptional profile to those that are known to participate in COVID-19.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of single-cell atlases.

claim: 32 placental villi/decidua samples collected in the third trimester were pooled for snRNA-seq analysis.
source: therefore, we pooled 32 placental villi/decidua samples collected in the third trimester (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the study's methodology.
